neighbors.heading: who makes it grow?
neighbors.text: Today the farmer planted, slept, and the seed grew, he knew not how. The Qur'an asks the farmer a question: "Have ye seen that which ye cultivate? Is it ye who foster it, or are We the Fosterer?" You dig, you sow, you wait. The growing, the Qur'an says, belongs to God.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells the seed as a parable of God's kingdom, growing unseen. The Qur'an points to the real field as a sign of God's power, and adds that God could turn the crop to chaff, so the farmer stays grateful.
neighbors.shared: you plant, you rest, and the growing isn't all yours.

neighbors.heading: it grows while you sleep
neighbors.text: Today the seed grew while the farmer slept. Psychologists found something like it. John Jenkins and Karl Dallenbach had people learn nonsense syllables, then either sleep or stay awake. After the same hours, the sleepers remembered more. Later research suggests the sleeping brain sorts and keeps what the day planted. You do the work; rest does some too.
neighbors.difference: Mark tells the story about God's kingdom, and the growing belongs to God. The psychology describes a brain at work in the dark, and makes no claim about God either way.
neighbors.shared: some of the best growing happens once you stop pushing.
neighbors.sources: Jenkins & Dallenbach, "Obliviscence during sleep and waking" (1924) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: after the prayer, the kitchen
neighbors.text: Today the miracle ended with: give her something to eat. Sikhs build that into the gurdwara. Beside the prayer hall is the langar, a free kitchen where anyone, of any faith or none, sits on the floor side by side and is fed. The Guru Granth Sahib praises the one who works for what they eat and gives some of it away.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the meal follows a miracle Christians read as Jesus's power over death. For Sikhs, the langar isn't a sign of power but everyday seva, a practice they trace to Guru Nanak, where no one is served above anyone else.
neighbors.shared: holy moments end at the table, with someone fed.

neighbors.heading: the guest is a god
neighbors.text: Today, after the girl got up, Jesus said: give her something to eat. Hindu homes carry a teaching about the person who needs feeding. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells the student leaving his teacher: let your mother be a god to you, your father, your teacher, and your guest. Atithi devo bhava. Feeding someone is a way of honoring the sacred.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the food comes after Jesus raises a child, and Christians read it as a sign of his power over death. In the Upanishad, honoring the guest is a householder's daily duty, tied to no miracle.
neighbors.shared: a hungry person at your table is never an interruption.

neighbors.heading: it starts in the mind
neighbors.text: Today Jesus moved the question from the plate to the heart. The Dhammapada begins in the same place: "All that we are is the result of what we have thought." And: "If a man speaks or acts with an evil thought, pain follows him, as the wheel follows the foot of the ox that draws the carriage."
neighbors.difference: For Jesus, what comes out of the heart is what defiles a person before God. The Buddha speaks of no creator: harmful thoughts bring suffering by cause and effect, and the mind can be trained clear.
neighbors.shared: what comes out of you starts long before you speak.

neighbors.heading: thought, word and deed
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said evil comes from within, out of the heart. Catholics carry that into an old prayer of confession, the Confiteor, which admits sin "in thought, word, and deed." The thought comes first. The Church teaches that sin is rooted in the heart, and invites an examination of conscience before confession.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read this teaching. Catholics also bring what the heart has done to the sacrament of confession, where a priest speaks God's forgiveness; many Protestants confess straight to God, without a priest.
neighbors.shared: the cleaning starts on the inside, where no one else can see.
neighbors.sources: Confiteor (traditional English) · Catechism of the Catholic Church 1853 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: faith that makes the fact
neighbors.text: Today a father prayed: Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. The psychologist William James defended starting with half. In "The Will to Believe" he argued that some things only come true if we move toward them before we're sure: "faith in a fact can help create the fact." Trusting a friendship, he said, is often what makes it real.
neighbors.difference: The father brings his half-faith to Jesus and asks him to make up the rest. James wrote as a philosopher about any belief, and didn't say who, if anyone, fills the gap.
neighbors.shared: you can start with the half you have.

neighbors.heading: how long? and still, trust
neighbors.text: Today a father cried: I believe; help my unbelief. Psalm 13 holds both in one prayer. It opens: "How long, O LORD, wilt Thou forget me for ever?" A few lines later: "But as for me, in Thy mercy do I trust." Jewish prayer has room for the question and the trust, said to God in one breath.
neighbors.difference: In Mark, the father brings his doubt to Jesus, and Christians read the healing as Jesus's answer. Jews pray the psalm directly to God, and the psalm itself ends in trust before any answer comes.
neighbors.shared: doubt and trust can share one honest prayer.

neighbors.heading: let go, then enjoy
neighbors.text: Today Jesus looked at a man, loved him, and asked him to give it all away. The Isha Upanishad opens on the same theme. It says all this world is dwelt in by the Lord; let go of it, and then enjoy, and do not covet anyone's wealth. Some Hindus take that to its end in sannyasa, leaving property behind entirely.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks one man to sell everything and follow him. The Upanishad speaks to everyone, and the letting go is first inward; many Hindus live it as householders, holding what they have loosely rather than giving it all away.
neighbors.shared: what you hold loosely can't hold you.

neighbors.heading: spend what you love
neighbors.text: Today Jesus asked a rich man to give to the poor, and he went away grieved. The Qur'an sets a similar bar: "Ye will not attain unto piety until ye spend of that which ye love. And whatsoever ye spend, Allah is aware thereof." Giving the leftovers is easy. The test is the thing you'd rather keep.
neighbors.difference: Jesus asks this one man for everything, and to follow him. Islam sets a yearly share, zakat, for every Muslim with enough wealth, and the Prophet advised a man not to give away so much that his family would be left in need.
neighbors.shared: the gift that costs you something says the most.
neighbors.sources: Qur'an 3:92 (Pickthall 1930) · Sahih al-Bukhari 2742, Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas and his bequest (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: servant of the servants
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said he came not to be served, but to serve. Catholics act it out on Holy Thursday, when in many parishes the priest kneels and washes people's feet, as Jesus did. And an old title of the pope carries the same idea: servus servorum Dei, servant of the servants of God.
neighbors.difference: Christians share this verse. Catholics also see it lived through the ordained ministry, with the pope and bishops holding real authority that they're called to use as service; many Protestants stress the servanthood of every believer, with no pope.
neighbors.shared: the best seat is the one you give up for someone else.
neighbors.sources: Mark 10:45 · Roman Missal, Holy Thursday washing of feet (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the work of the hands
neighbors.text: Today Jesus turned the best seats upside down: the first must be servant of all. Sikhs call that seva, selfless service. In the gurdwara, anyone might be scrubbing pots, sweeping the floor, or handing out roti. The Guru Granth Sahib says that by serving in this world, a person is given a place of honor in the Lord's court.
neighbors.difference: Jesus speaks of giving his life as a ransom for many, which Christians see as his alone. In Sikhism, seva isn't one person's sacrifice for others; it's every Sikh's daily path, done humbly, to wear away the ego.
neighbors.shared: serving well never made anyone smaller.

neighbors.heading: hear, O Israel
neighbors.text: Today Jesus answered from his own people's scripture. Jews still pray it, morning and night: "Hear, O Israel: the LORD our God, the LORD is one. And thou shalt love the LORD thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy might." The words go on the doorpost, in the mezuzah, as Deuteronomy says.
neighbors.difference: For Jews, the Shema is the heart of God's covenant with Israel, lived through the commandments. Christians hear it through Jesus, and most confess God as Trinity, which Jews do not; both say God is one.
neighbors.shared: love God, love the person beside you: an old pair, still together.

neighbors.heading: as yourself
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to love your neighbor as yourself. The Buddha built kindness on that same "as yourself." The Dhammapada says everyone trembles at harm and everyone loves life; see that others are like you, and do no harm. Buddhists grow it into metta, loving-kindness, wished for every being, the way a mother guards her only child.
neighbors.difference: Jesus joins love of neighbor to love of one God. The Buddha's teaching doesn't rest on a creator; kindness grows from seeing that every being, like you, wants to be happy and free of pain.
neighbors.shared: the person next to you wants what you want: to be safe.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada 129–130 (paraphrase) · Karaniya Metta Sutta, Sutta Nipata 1.8 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: despair not
neighbors.text: Today Peter denied his friend three times, then wept. Islam has a door for that moment: tawba, turning back. The Qur'an says: "O My slaves who have been prodigal to their own hurt! Despair not of the mercy of Allah, Who forgiveth all sins. Lo! He is the Forgiving, the Merciful."
neighbors.difference: Christians read Peter's tears in the light of Jesus, who later restores him; for them, forgiveness comes through Christ. In Islam, a person turns directly to Allah, and sincere tawba is accepted.
neighbors.shared: falling hard isn't the end; turning back is the start.

neighbors.heading: guilt, not shame
neighbors.text: Today Peter wept, and the weeping was where he started again. Psychologist June Tangney's research draws a line here. Guilt says: I did a bad thing. Shame says: I am bad. In her studies, people prone to guilt tended to apologize and repair, while people prone to shame tended to hide or lash out.
neighbors.difference: Mark tells Peter's tears inside a larger story of Jesus's forgiveness. The psychology names no forgiver; it shows only that regret aimed at what you did, not at who you are, helps people make things right.
neighbors.shared: a failure can be something you did, not who you are.

neighbors.heading: your will is sweet
neighbors.text: Today Jesus prayed a psalm from the cross, and the women stayed. Sikhs remember their own Guru in agony. Tradition says that Guru Arjan, tortured in Lahore, held to the words of his own hymn: your doing seems sweet to me; Nanak begs only for the treasure of the Name. Sikhs honor him as a martyr.
neighbors.difference: Jesus's cry asks God why. Guru Arjan's line accepts God's will as sweet. Christians see Jesus's death as saving the world; Sikhs honor the Guru's death as courage for truth, not a sacrifice for sin.
neighbors.shared: even in the worst hour, the prayer still goes to God.

neighbors.heading: a cry in the hall
neighbors.text: Today Jesus cried out: my God, why hast thou forsaken me? The Mahabharata has a cry like it. Draupadi is dragged into the gambling hall, and her husbands and most of the elders sit silent. In the telling many Hindus know, she calls on Krishna, and as they pull at her sari, it keeps on coming, without end.
neighbors.difference: In that telling, Krishna answers at once and saves Draupadi's honor. In Mark, no rescue comes: Jesus dies, and Christians read that silence as part of God's saving love, answered on the third day.
neighbors.shared: when everyone else goes silent, the cry still has somewhere to go.
neighbors.sources: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, the dice game (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: a mustard seed for grief
neighbors.text: Today Jesus blessed those who mourn. Buddhists tell of Kisa Gotami, carrying her dead child, begging the Buddha for medicine. Bring me a mustard seed, he said, from a house where no one has died. She went door to door. Every house had lost someone. She laid her child to rest, and her grief found company.
neighbors.difference: Jesus promises comfort, someone called to your side. The Buddha's comfort is seeing clearly that loss touches every house and that all things change; it doesn't rest on a promise from God.
neighbors.shared: yours is not the only house that has known loss.
neighbors.sources: Dhammapada commentary on verse 114, story of Kisa Gotami (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: the mother who stayed
neighbors.text: Today Jesus blessed those who mourn. Catholics keep a picture of that grief: Mary at the cross. An old hymn, the Stabat Mater, sings: "At the cross her station keeping, stood the mournful Mother weeping, close to Jesus to the last." Catholics honor her as Our Lady of Sorrows, a mother who knows.
neighbors.difference: All Christians remember Mary at the cross; John's Gospel puts her there. Catholics also ask her to pray for them in their grief and keep a feast of her sorrows; many Protestants honor her but pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: someone who has wept will sit beside you while you weep.
neighbors.sources: Stabat Mater, tr. Edward Caswall (1849) · John 19:25

neighbors.heading: the repair attempt
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: leave your gift at the altar, go, make it right first. Psychologist John Gottman studied couples and found that fighting alone doesn't predict a breakup. What matters is the repair attempt: a joke, a touch, a "let's start over." Couples who make repairs, and accept them, tend to last.
neighbors.difference: Jesus ties making peace with your neighbor to worship; the neighbor comes before the altar. Gottman's research is about relationships alone, and says nothing about God or worship.
neighbors.shared: the first step back toward someone is worth more than being right.
neighbors.sources: John Gottman, The Seven Principles for Making Marriage Work (1999) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: first, your neighbor
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to leave the gift at the altar and be reconciled first. The Mishnah teaches something close about Yom Kippur: the Day of Atonement atones for wrongs between a person and God, but for wrongs against another person, it doesn't atone until you make peace with them. So before Yom Kippur, many Jews go and ask forgiveness.
neighbors.difference: Jesus tells it as a story about a gift at the altar, and Christians hear it as his teaching. In Judaism it's law, tied to the yearly Day of Atonement, and later rabbis say to ask more than once if refused.
neighbors.shared: the person you hurt comes before the prayer.

neighbors.heading: the hidden gift
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said to give so quietly your left hand doesn't know what your right is doing. Hindus have a name for that: gupt daan, a secret gift, given without your name on it. The Bhagavad Gita calls the purest, sattvic gift the one given simply because giving is right, to someone who can't repay, at the right time and place.
neighbors.difference: Jesus says the Father who sees in secret will reward. The Gita praises giving with no thought of reward at all, a duty done for its own sake, and many Hindus offer the gift to God.
neighbors.shared: the best gifts don't need a name card.

neighbors.heading: the left hand doesn't know
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth. Muslims know almost the same words. The Prophet named seven whom God shades on a day with no other shade; one gives charity so secretly that his left hand doesn't know what his right gave. The Qur'an: "If ye hide it and give it to the poor, it will be better for you."
neighbors.difference: Jesus teaches this as his own word. In Islam the saying is the Prophet Muhammad's, and the Qur'an also calls open giving good, since zakat is a public duty; secret giving is praised as better.
neighbors.shared: God sees the gift no one else did.
neighbors.sources: Sahih al-Bukhari 1423 and Sahih Muslim 1031, the seven given shade (paraphrase) · Qur'an 2:271 (Pickthall 1930)

neighbors.heading: my little sisters the birds
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: behold the fowls of the air. Francis of Assisi took him at his word. The Little Flowers of St. Francis tells of him preaching to a flock of birds: you sow not and reap not, he told them, and God feeds you, so praise him. The birds, the story goes, stayed still until he blessed them.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read Jesus's words about the birds. Catholics also hold up Francis, a canonized saint, as a living picture of them and honor him as patron of ecology; many Protestants admire Francis without asking saints' prayers.
neighbors.shared: look closely at a bird, and worry gets a little smaller.
neighbors.sources: The Little Flowers of St. Francis, ch. 16 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: who feeds the young ones?
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said: behold the birds, God feeds them. Sikhs pray something close every evening, in Rehras. The kunj birds fly hundreds of miles, leaving their young behind. Who feeds them? Who teaches them to feed themselves? So why, O mind, do you scheme and worry, when the Lord himself provides?
neighbors.difference: Jesus calls God Father and says you are worth more than the birds. The Guru's hymn speaks of the one Creator who cares for every creature, and invites remembering the Name, Naam, in place of worry.
neighbors.shared: the one who feeds the birds has not forgotten you.

neighbors.heading: we will do, and we will hear
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said the wise builder hears and does. At Sinai, Exodus says, the people answered: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. Doing comes first. Pirkei Avot says it plainly: not study but doing is the main thing.
neighbors.difference: Jesus calls his own sayings the rock to build on. For Jews, the doing is the Torah's commandments, kept as a people in covenant with God, and study itself counts as one of them.
neighbors.shared: the house stands on what you do, not just what you heard.

neighbors.heading: a flower with no scent
neighbors.text: Today Jesus said hearing isn't enough; the wise build by doing. The Dhammapada puts it in a picture: "Like a beautiful flower, full of colour, but without scent, are the fine but fruitless words of him who does not act accordingly." Lovely to look at. Nothing that lasts.
neighbors.difference: Jesus points to his own words as the rock, with God as judge. The Buddha asked followers to test his teaching in practice, and freedom comes through their own effort, not a creator's verdict.
neighbors.shared: words you live outlast words you only admire.

neighbors.heading: everything is praising
neighbors.text: Today Francis praised God for brother sun and sister water. The Qur'an hears creation singing too: "The seven heavens and the earth and all that is therein praise Him, and there is not a thing but hymneth His praise; but ye understand not their praise." Sun, rain, stone: each praising in its own way.
neighbors.difference: Francis calls sun and water brother and sister, family to us. The Qur'an speaks of creatures as signs, ayat, pointing to God, and of people as trustees of the earth.
neighbors.shared: the whole world was praying long before we joined in.

neighbors.heading: hitched to everything else
neighbors.text: Today Francis called the sun his brother and the earth his sister. John Muir, walking the Sierra Nevada, put it as a naturalist: "When we try to pick out anything by itself, we find it hitched to everything else in the Universe." For Muir, kinship with the living world was simply what close looking shows.
neighbors.difference: Francis praises God through every creature, and the kinship flows from one Maker. Muir's line rests on watching nature closely, and asks no one to share a creed.
neighbors.shared: you are kin to the water you drink.
neighbors.sources: John Muir, My First Summer in the Sierra (1911)

neighbors.heading: hands at work, heart with God
neighbors.text: Today Brother Lawrence turned his omelet for the love of God. Sikh teaching makes that a daily rule: kirat karo, work honestly, and naam japo, remember God. A line from the saint Namdev, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says: with your hands and feet do all your work, and keep your mind with the Pure Lord.
neighbors.difference: Brother Lawrence lived as a lay brother in a monastery. Sikhism asks for the same in ordinary family life; the Gurus turned away from monastic withdrawal, so work, family and prayer belong together.
neighbors.shared: God is as near at the stove as at the altar.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Saloks of Kabir, Namdev's line (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: whatever you do, offer it
neighbors.text: Today Brother Lawrence found God among the pots. Krishna says something close in the Bhagavad Gita: whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer or give, do it as an offering to me. Hindus call this karma yoga, the way of action: ordinary work, done without clutching at the result, becomes worship.
neighbors.difference: Brother Lawrence talked with God in plain words while he worked, as with a friend. Krishna's teaching adds letting go of the fruit of action: do the work, offer it, and don't cling to how it turns out.
neighbors.shared: the dishes can be a prayer, if you let them.

neighbors.heading: come back, gently
neighbors.text: Today the mystics' secret turned out to be attention, held for years. The Buddha taught it as mindfulness, sati: noticing the breath, the body, feelings and the mind, just as they are. When the mind wanders, you notice, and come back. In the Satipatthana Sutta he calls this a direct path past sorrow.
neighbors.difference: Christian mystics pay attention to God, to someone who loves them back. Buddhist mindfulness pays attention to what is happening here and now, and its goal is clear seeing and freedom, not meeting a God.
neighbors.shared: every deep thing begins with simply noticing.

neighbors.heading: where was God today?
neighbors.text: Today the mystics turned out to be people who paid attention for years. Catholics have a nightly way in: the Examen, from Ignatius of Loyola. You look back over the day with thanks, and ask where God was in it, where you turned away, and what tomorrow needs. A few minutes, every night, that train you to notice.
neighbors.difference: Many Christians reflect on their day. The Examen comes from a Catholic saint and the Jesuit order, and Catholics often pair it with confession; other churches use it too, sometimes without the sacrament.
neighbors.shared: a day looked back on kindly is a day you really lived.

neighbors.heading: by their fruits
neighbors.text: Today John Wesley's heart was strangely warmed. Later, the psychologist William James gathered stories like that in The Varieties of Religious Experience. He took such moments seriously, as real experiences that change how people live, and judged them, borrowing Jesus's words, by their fruits: did the life grow kinder, braver, more whole?
neighbors.difference: For Wesley, the warmth was assurance from God that Christ had taken away his sins. James, as a psychologist, studied what such experiences do in a life, and left open where they come from.
neighbors.shared: a warmed heart shows in the life that follows.
neighbors.sources: William James, The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902) (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: God wants the heart
neighbors.text: Today Wesley's heart was strangely warmed, and Methodists asked each other: how is it with your soul? The Talmud has a short saying: Rachmana liba ba'i, the Merciful One wants the heart. Jewish prayer has a word for that inner turn, kavanah, intention: saying the words with your heart in them.
neighbors.difference: Wesley's warmth came as trust in Christ for salvation. In Judaism the heart is given to God through prayer and the commandments themselves, done with kavanah.
neighbors.shared: the words matter more when your heart is in them.

neighbors.heading: born of joy
neighbors.text: Today Genesis said God saw everything he had made, and it was very good. The Taittiriya Upanishad tells of a seeker, Bhrigu, who searched for where the world comes from, and found at last: from bliss, ananda, beings are born; by bliss they live; into bliss they go at the end.
neighbors.difference: In Genesis, God makes a world distinct from himself; Christians teach he made it from nothing. In the Upanishad, beings come from Brahman, bliss itself, and return to it; the world isn't set apart from its source in the same way.
neighbors.shared: the world began in goodness, not by accident.

neighbors.heading: everything made good
neighbors.text: Today Genesis said creation was very good. The Qur'an speaks of God "Who made all things good which He created, and He began the creation of man from clay." It also tells of the heavens and the earth made in six days, as Genesis does.
neighbors.difference: Genesis says God rested on the seventh day. The Qur'an says no weariness touched God in creating, and Muslims keep no sabbath of rest; Friday is their day of gathered prayer.
neighbors.shared: you were made on purpose, and the making was good.

neighbors.heading: a friend who prays for you
neighbors.text: Today the creed spoke of the communion of saints. Catholics live it in prayer: they ask Mary and the saints to pray for them, the way you'd ask a friend. On All Saints' Day the Church remembers them all, and the next day, All Souls', it prays for those who have died.
neighbors.difference: All Christians say this line of the creed. Catholics ask the saints' prayers and pray for the souls in purgatory; many Protestants honor the saints as examples and pray to God alone.
neighbors.shared: death doesn't end the family.

neighbors.heading: remembered in every prayer
neighbors.text: Today the creed said the living and the dead are one family. Sikhs feel that whenever they pray Ardas, the standing prayer. It remembers the Gurus by name, then the Sikhs who gave their lives, who served, who kept faith, and asks the gathering to call them to mind. The sangat, the holy company, holds past and present together.
neighbors.difference: Catholics ask the saints to pray for them. Sikhs don't pray to the Gurus' companions or the martyrs; they remember them, and the prayer itself is offered to Waheguru, the one God.
neighbors.shared: the people who kept faith before you are remembered when you pray.

neighbors.heading: we have sinned
neighbors.text: Today Paul quoted the Psalms: there is none righteous, no, not one. The Hebrew Bible says it too: "For there is not a righteous man upon earth, that doeth good, and sinneth not." On Yom Kippur, Jews confess together, in the plural: we have sinned, we have betrayed. Not I alone. We.
neighbors.difference: Paul builds from this toward grace through Christ, and many Christians speak of original sin. Judaism doesn't teach original sin; each person has a good and a bad inclination, and can always turn back, teshuvah.
neighbors.shared: nobody gets to stand on the balcony and look down.

neighbors.heading: the three roots
neighbors.text: Today Paul said none is righteous, no, not one. The Buddha named three roots of what goes wrong in us: greed, hatred and delusion. They grow in every untrained mind, not just in the people we'd like to blame. The Dhammapada adds a familiar warning: the faults of others are easy to see; our own are hard to see.
neighbors.difference: Paul speaks of sin against God, healed by God's grace. The Buddha speaks of unwholesome roots, not sin against a creator; they are pulled up through understanding and practice.
neighbors.shared: the finger that points out can point back at us too.

neighbors.heading: with hardship, ease
neighbors.text: Today Paul said trouble grows patience, character and hope. The Qur'an calls that patience sabr: "Give glad tidings to the steadfast, Who say, when a misfortune striketh them: Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning." And it promises, twice in a row: "Lo! with hardship goeth ease."
neighbors.difference: Paul grounds hope in God's love, shown in Christ dying for sinners. The Qur'an grounds it in trust that everything returns to Allah, who tests people and rewards the patient.
neighbors.shared: hard days can grow something easy ones can't.

neighbors.heading: growth after the storm
neighbors.text: Today Paul traced a chain: trouble, endurance, tested character, hope. Psychologists Richard Tedeschi and Lawrence Calhoun named what many people report after a hard season: post-traumatic growth. Not that suffering is good, but that some come out with closer friendships, new strength, and a clearer sense of what matters.
neighbors.difference: Paul says hope doesn't disappoint because God's love has been poured into the heart. The psychology describes growth some people find, not all, and makes no promise about why.
neighbors.shared: pain doesn't get to be the whole story of a hard season.

neighbors.heading: answer evil with good
neighbors.text: Today Paul said: overcome evil with good. Sheikh Farid, whose verses are kept in the Guru Granth Sahib, says it close: Farid, answer evil with goodness; don't fill your mind with anger. Then, he says, your body won't fall sick, and you'll gain everything.
neighbors.difference: Paul quotes Proverbs and leaves vengeance to God, in the light of Christ's love for enemies. For Sikhs, Farid's line is Gurbani, and Sikh teaching also honors defending the weak, so goodness never means letting injustice go.
neighbors.shared: kindness to someone who wronged you can change two people.
neighbors.sources: Guru Granth Sahib, Saloks of Sheikh Farid, Ang 1381–1382 (paraphrase)

neighbors.heading: win anger with calm
neighbors.text: Today Paul said to overcome evil with good. In the Mahabharata, the wise counselor Vidura gives a teaching still widely quoted: conquer anger with calm, the wicked with goodness, the miser with giving, and the liar with truth.
neighbors.difference: Paul ties it to God's judgment and Christ's love for enemies. Vidura gives it as counsel about dharma, right living, and the Mahabharata also honors those who must fight for justice.
neighbors.shared: the answer to harm doesn't have to look like harm.

neighbors.heading: the sisters' songs
neighbors.text: Today Paul greeted Phoebe and named the women of the church one by one. Buddhists keep an old book of women's voices: the Therigatha, verses of the elder nuns. Each poem comes under a name, Patacara, Kisa Gotami, Mutta, and many tell how she found freedom, often after grief.
neighbors.difference: Paul's women serve a church gathered around Christ. The nuns of the Therigatha speak of awakening through their own practice, freedom from craving, with no creator in view.
neighbors.shared: every name on the list was a whole life.

neighbors.heading: names said at the altar
neighbors.text: Today Paul ended his letter with names, many of them women. Catholics still say names at the altar. The Roman Canon, an ancient prayer of the Mass, remembers saints by name, among them Felicity, Perpetua, Agatha, Lucy, Agnes, Cecilia and Anastasia. And Phoebe herself is listed among the Church's saints.
neighbors.difference: All Christians read Romans 16. Catholics also name saints in the Mass and ask their prayers; many Protestant churches remember them as examples, without asking their prayers.
neighbors.shared: being remembered by name is a kind of love.
neighbors.sources: Roman Missal, Eucharistic Prayer I (the Roman Canon) · Roman Martyrology, 3 September (paraphrase)
